title: Coroutines: Builders (launch, async, runBlocking, withContext, scope builders, CoroutineStart)
scopeHtml: Scope: how each coroutine builder starts work, returns results, waits for children, and where it bites in production. Dispatchers, Job internals, cancellation and exception propagation are covered in their own sections and only cross-referenced here. Versions: Kotlin 2.x, kotlinx.coroutines 1.9 to 1.11.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between launch and async? When do you pick one over the other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first filter question. They want to hear about return types, how results come back, and a hint that the two report failures differently, not "async is for parallel stuff".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both are extension functions on CoroutineScope that start a child coroutine and return right away. launch returns a Job, which is a handle with no result, so I use it for fire-and-forget work like "save this, then update state". async returns a Deferred<T>, which is a Job that also carries a result. I call await() to suspend until the value is ready. I use async only when I need a value back and want to run several of those at the same time. For a single value on another thread I use withContext, not async { }.await().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Both builders take context, start and a suspend block. Both create a coroutine whose Job becomes a child of the scope's Job, which is structured concurrency.
  • launch: block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit returns Job. The result is Unit. Completion means the body finished and so did all of its children.
  • async: block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> T returns Deferred<T>. Deferred<T> : Job adds await(), getCompleted() (experimental) and onAwait (for select).
  • Failure reporting differs. That is covered in depth in the exception-handling section. In short:
    • An uncaught exception in launch goes up to the parent. At a root launch it goes to a CoroutineExceptionHandler or the thread's uncaught-exception handler, which crashes an Android app.
    • async also stores the exception inside the Deferred and rethrows it from await().
    • Both still cancel a regular (non-supervisor) parent when they fail, whether or not anyone awaits.
launch async
Returns Job Deferred<T> (is-a Job)
Result none await()
Typical use side effects, UI updates, collecting concurrent value-producing work
Failure surfaced via parent / handler parent and await()

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// launch: side effect, no value
viewModelScope.launch {
    repo.markRead(id)
    _state.update { it.copy(read = true) }
}

// async: two values computed concurrently
viewModelScope.launch {
    val profile = async { api.profile() }
    val feed = async { api.feed() }
    _state.value = Ui(profile.await(), feed.await())
}

// Anti-pattern: async used only to wait for its result straight away
val user = async(Dispatchers.IO) { db.user() }.await()   // use withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { db.user() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking async is "more parallel" than launch. Both are just as concurrent. Parallelism comes from the dispatcher.
  • Using async for side effects and never awaiting. Any failure is then only seen through the parent.
  • Believing an exception in an un-awaited async stays silent. Inside coroutineScope it still cancels the parent.
  • Returning a Deferred from a repository API. Expose a suspend fun instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Deferred a Job? → Yes. You can cancel(), join() and inspect isActive on it. join() waits for completion but does not throw the failure, while await() does.
  2. Can I call await() twice? → Yes. Every later call returns the same cached value, or rethrows the same exception.
  3. Why is async { }.await() straight away worse than withContext? → It allocates an extra coroutine and Deferred, and it adds a level to the job tree that the failure must travel through. withContext does the same thing in one step and returns the value directly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "launch for no result, async for a result". The senior adds that both are children under structured concurrency and that failure goes up the tree even without await. They name the withContext alternative and say that Deferred should not leak through public APIs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A common review finding is async used everywhere "for speed" and never awaited. Crashes then show up as JobCancellationException in unrelated sibling coroutines, and the real cause is hard to trace.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does Deferred.await() do? What happens if the deferred already finished, failed, or was cancelled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you know await suspends rather than blocks, caches its outcome, and is cancellable on the waiting side.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: await() suspends the calling coroutine until the Deferred completes. It never blocks the thread. If the deferred already succeeded, it returns the value at once. If it failed, await() rethrows that exception. If it was cancelled, await() throws CancellationException. The outcome is stored, so every caller gets the same result. If the coroutine that is waiting gets cancelled, its await() throws, but the deferred keeps running. Only the waiter stops.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Deferred completes in one of three ways: with a value, with an exception, or by being cancelled. Each await() registers a completion handler, much like suspendCancellableCoroutine, and resumes when the deferred finishes.
  • Fast path: if isCompleted is already true, await() does not suspend at all.
  • Waiting is cancellable. Cancelling the awaiting coroutine removes its handler and throws CancellationException in the waiter. It does not cancel the Deferred. The two are separate jobs.
  • await() versus join(): join() waits but never throws the deferred's failure. Its only exception is the caller's own cancellation.
  • Stack traces: the exception rethrown by await() is the original one. In debug mode, stack-trace recovery may add a copy with the awaiting frame (see the debugging section).
caller --await()--> [Deferred: Active] ----completes----> resume(value)
                                    \---fails(e)-------> resumeWithException(e)
                                    \---cancelled------> throw CancellationException
caller cancelled while waiting --> caller gets CancellationException, Deferred untouched

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val d = scope.async { compute() }
val a = d.await()   // suspends
val b = d.await()   // returns the same value, no recomputation

// Failure is rethrown at the await site
val bad = supervisorScope { async { error("boom") } }
runCatching { bad.await() }   // Result.failure(IllegalStateException("boom"))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing await() restarts the work. It never does. The computation runs once.
  • Wrapping await() in try/catch and thinking that isolates the failure. Inside a regular coroutineScope the parent is already being cancelled (see the exception section).
  • Catching Exception around await() swallows CancellationException (see the cancellation section).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does await() block the thread? → No. It suspends. Blocking would need runBlocking { d.await() }.
  2. What is getCompleted()? → An experimental, non-suspending getter. It throws IllegalStateException if the deferred is not complete yet. Rarely justified.
  3. Two coroutines await the same deferred and one is cancelled. What happens to the other? → Nothing. Waiters are independent, and the deferred is cancelled only through its own Job.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it waits for the result". The senior covers suspend versus block, the cached outcome, independent waiters versus cancelling the deferred, and the difference from join().

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen-level waiter is cancelled when the user navigates away, while a shared Deferred in an app scope keeps running. That is the right design for deduplicating requests (see A1-Q293).

questions.promptHtml: What does withContext do? Is it a new coroutine? What does it cost when the dispatcher does not change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: withContext is the most used builder in Android code. They want to know you understand "switch, run, come back, return a value" and its fast paths.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: withContext(ctx) { } is a suspend function. It runs the block with the current context merged with ctx, suspends the caller until the block and all of its children finish, then returns the block's result on the original context. With a different dispatcher it dispatches into that dispatcher and dispatches back afterwards. With the same dispatcher it skips the dispatch and just runs the block, so it is cheap. Its main job is to make a function main-safe: suspend fun load() = withContext(io) { ... }.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Signature: suspend fun <T> withContext(context: CoroutineContext, block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> T): T.
  • It creates a scoped coroutine, an internal ScopeCoroutine subtype, whose Job is a child of the caller's job. So yes, it is technically a new coroutine with its own Job, but it is sequential: the caller waits.
  • Three paths in the implementation, simplified:
    1. The new context equals the old one: run the block in place as an undispatched scope.
    2. The dispatcher is the same and only other elements changed (for example CoroutineName): run in place, no dispatch.
    3. The dispatcher is different: start the block on the new dispatcher and resume the caller through its original dispatcher when done.
  • It behaves like coroutineScope: it waits for all children, and a child failure cancels the block and rethrows.
  • Before returning, it checks cancellation. If the caller was cancelled, the result is thrown away (see A1-Q289).
  • kotlinx.coroutines 1.7.0 reduced its thread-local and performance overhead (changelog #3592).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileRepo(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher, private val dao: ProfileDao) {
    // main-safe: callers on Main can call this directly
    suspend fun load(id: String): Profile = withContext(io) {
        dao.byId(id) ?: Profile.EMPTY
    }
}

// Redundant: Room's suspend DAO is already main-safe; this adds a context switch, no benefit
suspend fun loadRedundant(id: String) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.suspendById(id) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping already main-safe suspend calls (Retrofit suspend, Room suspend) in withContext(IO) "just in case".
  • Using withContext inside a tight loop with a different dispatcher. Each iteration pays two dispatches. Switch once around the whole loop.
  • Expecting withContext to run in parallel. It is sequential, so use async to get parallelism.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. withContext(Dispatchers.Main) while already on Main: does it post to the Looper? → With Dispatchers.Main and the same dispatcher instance, it takes the no-dispatch fast path. Switching between Main and Main.immediate is a different dispatcher, and immediate avoids posting when already on the main thread (see the dispatchers section).
  2. Does withContext(Job()) work? → It breaks the parent link and therefore structured cancellation. Covered in the Job section. Don't do it.
  3. withContext versus coroutineScope? → Same waiting and failure semantics. coroutineScope keeps the context and only creates a scope for child builders.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it switches threads". The senior says it returns a value, waits for its children, has no-dispatch fast paths, checks cancellation on exit, and is the tool for main-safety, not for parallelism.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that put withContext(IO) around every repository call, on top of a withContext(IO) in the data source, saw thousands of extra dispatches per scroll in method traces. The fix was to own the dispatcher switch at one layer.

questions.promptHtml: What does runBlocking do, and where is it actually acceptable to use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a red-flag detector. Using runBlocking in app code to "call a suspend function from a non-suspend place" is a classic source of ANRs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: runBlocking starts a coroutine and blocks the current thread until that coroutine and all of its children finish, then returns the result. It is the bridge from blocking code into coroutines. It is fine in a main() function, in some framework callbacks that must be synchronous and already run on a background thread, and in older tests (today I use runTest). In Android app code on the main thread it is wrong: it freezes the UI and can deadlock. Inside another coroutine it is also wrong, because it blocks a pool thread.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Signature (JVM): fun <T> runBlocking(context: CoroutineContext = EmptyCoroutineContext, block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> T): T. It is not a suspend function.
  • If no dispatcher is given, it creates an event loop on the calling thread. Children launched inside without their own dispatcher run on that same thread, interleaved through the event loop.
  • It parks the thread until the root coroutine completes, then returns the value or rethrows the exception.
  • If the thread is interrupted, it is cancelled. 1.10.2 fixed a case where an interrupted thread could fail to run the coroutine to completion (#4399). 1.11.0 added a callsInPlace(EXACTLY_ONCE) contract, so val can be assigned inside the block.
Place OK? Why
fun main() / CLI / scripts Yes The program has nothing else to do while waiting
Unit tests Legacy runTest gives virtual time and catches leaks
Background thread required to be synchronous (e.g. OkHttp Interceptor/Authenticator, ContentProvider on a binder thread) Carefully It blocks that thread, so bound it with a timeout and never hold locks
Android main thread No Freezes the UI, ANR after about 5 s of input timeout, deadlock risk
Inside a coroutine / suspend fun No Blocks a pool worker, starvation (A1-Q291)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// OK: a JVM tool
fun main() = runBlocking {
    val (a, b) = awaitAll(async { fetchA() }, async { fetchB() })
    println(a + b)
}

// BAD: Activity main thread
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    val config = runBlocking { configRepo.load() }   // UI frozen until network/disk completes
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it to "make it compile" when calling a suspend function from a callback. Restructure instead: launch in an owned scope.
  • Using it in Application.onCreate to load config. Every cold start then pays that latency, and startup ANRs follow.
  • Assuming runBlocking(Dispatchers.IO) { } on the main thread is fine. The main thread still waits, blocked.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. runBlocking versus coroutineScope? → Both wait for their children. runBlocking blocks the thread, while coroutineScope suspends and frees the thread.
  2. Why not in tests anymore? → runTest skips delay, has a default timeout and reports uncaught exceptions (see the testing section).
  3. Is runBlocking available in common or JS code? → Not on JS. It exists on JVM and Native, which is why the 1.11 contract was added in JVM+Native shared code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "don't use it on the main thread". The senior describes the thread-local event loop, lists the narrow cases where it is legitimate (sync framework callbacks off the main thread, with timeouts), and names the starvation risk inside pools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: runBlocking in Application.onCreate to read a DataStore value is one of the most common startup-ANR causes found in Play Console ANR clusters.

questions.promptHtml: listOf(a, b, c).awaitAll() versus a.await(); b.await(); c.await(). Is there any difference if all three are already running?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most people say "same thing". The senior answer understands fail-fast behaviour and how it depends on the scope type.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If all three are children of a regular coroutineScope, the end result is almost the same. Any failure cancels the scope and the siblings anyway. The difference shows when the deferreds are not tied together by a cancelling parent, for example in supervisorScope or when they come from another scope. Then sequential awaits wait for a even if c has already failed, so I only learn about the failure after the slowest earlier item finishes. awaitAll resumes with the first exception as soon as any deferred fails. awaitAll also starts lazy deferreds together, while sequential awaits start them one at a time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• awaitAll (an extension on Collection<Deferred<T>> and a vararg top-level function) resumes normally with the list of values once all of them complete. It resumes with the first exception, including cancellation, as soon as any completes exceptionally.
  • awaitAll does not cancel the others by itself. Cancelling siblings is the job of the parent scope. Inside supervisorScope the other deferreds keep running after awaitAll throws, unless I cancel them.
  • Implementation: it registers a completion handler on each deferred, and calls start() on each first, so LAZY ones run concurrently.
Timeline (supervisorScope, a=3s ok, b=1s ok, c fails at 0.5s)
sequential:  a.await() .......3s -> b.await() instant -> c.await() throws at t=3s
awaitAll:    throws at t=0.5s (a, b still running unless cancelled)
Situation Sequential awaits awaitAll
regular coroutineScope, one fails scope cancels, so effectively fail-fast fail-fast
supervisorScope / foreign deferreds failure seen after earlier awaits finish fail-fast at first failure
LAZY deferreds start one by one, so sequential all started, so concurrent
result type individual typed values List<T> (one common type)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadAll(ids: List<String>): List<Item> = coroutineScope {
    ids.map { id -> async { api.item(id) } }.awaitAll()
}

// Heterogeneous types: individual awaits read better, and inside coroutineScope it's still fail-fast
suspend fun header(): Header = coroutineScope {
    val user = async { api.user() }
    val badges = async { api.badges() }
    Header(user.await(), badges.await())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming awaitAll cancels the remaining deferreds on failure. It does not. The scope does.
  • map { async { } }.map { it.await() } with LAZY start turns parallel work into serial work.
  • Forcing different types into awaitAll with casts, List<Any>. Use individual awaits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Need partial results instead of fail-fast? → Use supervisorScope, map each to runCatching { it.await() }, and re-throw CancellationException (see A1-Q298).
  2. joinAll versus awaitAll? → joinAll waits for Jobs and ignores their failures. awaitAll returns values and throws.
  3. What is the order of the result list? → Same as the input order, regardless of which finished first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "awaitAll waits for all". The senior explains that fail-fast depends on the scope, that awaitAll itself does not cancel siblings, and how lazy start behaves.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: On a supervisor-based screen, a fast auth failure was only shown after a 10 s timeout on an unrelated image-metadata call, because the code awaited in declaration order.

questions.promptHtml: Compare coroutineScope, supervisorScope and withContext. When do you reach for each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These three scoped builders decide how failure spreads and how long a function takes to return. Mixing them up causes most "why did everything get cancelled" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: All three are suspend functions that create a child scope, run a block, wait for every child launched inside, and return the block's value. coroutineScope keeps the current context, and if any child fails it cancels all the other children and rethrows. supervisorScope has a SupervisorJob-like job, so a failing child does not cancel its siblings or the scope, and each child has to handle its own failure. withContext is coroutineScope plus a context change, usually a dispatcher. I use coroutineScope for all-or-nothing parallel decomposition, supervisorScope for independent tasks with partial results, and withContext to change thread or context for a sequential block.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
coroutineScope supervisorScope withContext(ctx)
Context inherited inherited, Job is supervisor-like inherited + ctx
Waits for children yes yes yes
Child fails cancels siblings and scope, rethrows siblings unaffected like coroutineScope
Body itself throws cancels children, rethrows cancels children, rethrows same
Typical use parallel all-or-nothing independent widgets / uploads main-safety, thread switch
  • A key detail of supervisorScope: a failed launch child is not rethrown by the scope. It goes to the CoroutineExceptionHandler in the context, or else the thread's uncaught-exception handler, which crashes an Android app. A failed async child holds its exception until await. Details are in the exception-handling section.
  • withContext(SupervisorJob()) is not a substitute for supervisorScope. Passing a Job breaks the parent link (see the Job section).
  • Waiting for children is what makes these builders "structured". The function cannot return while its work is still running, so no work leaks out of it (see A1-Q301 for the latency side effect).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// all-or-nothing: checkout needs both
suspend fun checkoutData() = coroutineScope {
    val cart = async { api.cart() }
    val address = async { api.address() }
    Checkout(cart.await(), address.await())
}

// independent: each tile may fail alone
suspend fun tiles(): List<Tile?> = supervisorScope {
    listOf(async { api.weather() }, async { api.news() })
        .map { d -> try { d.await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { null } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using supervisorScope with launch children and no handler, so one tile crashes the app.
  • Using coroutineScope for independent widgets, so one 500 response blanks the whole dashboard.
  • launch(SupervisorJob()) inside a scope, thinking it isolates the child. It detaches it instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does supervisorScope catch exceptions? → No. It only stops a child failure from cancelling siblings. The child still has to handle it.
  2. Is coroutineScope { } with no children free? → Nearly. It allocates a scope coroutine and runs undispatched in place.
  3. What happens if the caller of supervisorScope is cancelled? → Everything inside is cancelled. Supervision only goes downward.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "supervisor means children don't cancel each other". The senior adds where failed launch children go in a supervisor, that all three wait for children, and why passing SupervisorJob() as a context element is a different and broken thing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home screen moved from coroutineScope to supervisorScope and the "blank home screen" rate dropped, but crash rate went up because the tile children were launches without a handler. The fix was async plus per-tile result mapping.

questions.subtopic: async whose result is never awaited
questions.promptHtml: What happens to an async whose Deferred nobody ever awaits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand that async work runs on its own and that its failure path depends on the parent.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The work still runs. DEFAULT start means it is scheduled at once, whether or not anyone awaits. On success the value just sits in the Deferred until it is collected. On failure it depends on the parent. Under a regular Job or coroutineScope, the failure still cancels the parent and its siblings, so it is not silent. Under a SupervisorJob, supervisorScope or GlobalScope, the exception is held inside the Deferred and is never reported anywhere. Nothing crashes, no handler runs, no log. So an un-awaited async is either a side effect in disguise, which should be a launch, or a silent failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• async has no reporting channel of its own. Its exception is "handled" by storing it for await(). For the root or a supervisor child, the library treats Deferred as the owner, so CoroutineExceptionHandler is not invoked.
  • With a regular parent, the child's failure cancels the parent no matter what. Children always tell their parent when they fail.
  • Memory: the completed Deferred holds its result, or its exception and that exception's stack trace, until it is unreachable. Keeping un-awaited deferreds in a list keeps them alive.
  • A LAZY async that is never awaited or started never runs, and it keeps its parent from completing (A1-Q285).
Parent Success Failure, never awaited
coroutineScope / regular Job value dropped parent + siblings cancelled, exception rethrown up
supervisorScope / SupervisorJob value dropped silently lost
GlobalScope value dropped silently lost, and the coroutine is not tied to any lifecycle

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Silent failure: viewModelScope has a SupervisorJob
fun onRefresh() {
    viewModelScope.async { repo.sync() }   // if sync() throws, nobody ever knows
}

// Correct: it's a side effect, so use launch and handle failure explicitly
fun onRefreshFixed() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        try { repo.sync() } catch (e: IOException) { _events.trySend(Event.SyncFailed) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• viewModelScope.async { } used as a "safer launch". It hides crashes and also hides real bugs.
  • Lint: the Kotlin IDE warns about unused Deferred results in some cases. Treat that warning as a bug.
  • Thinking an un-awaited async inside coroutineScope is harmless. One failure tears down the whole scope.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does viewModelScope.async failure crash the app? → No. viewModelScope uses a SupervisorJob and nobody awaits, so it is silently lost.
  2. Does the computation get cancelled when the scope is cancelled? → Yes. It is a child either way.
  3. How would you detect these in a codebase? → Search for async { whose result is not assigned or awaited, enable the IDE inspection, and add a detekt or custom lint rule.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "the result is ignored". The senior lays out the failure behaviour per parent type, explains why CoroutineExceptionHandler never sees it, and recommends launch for side effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync feature "worked" in QA but silently failed for some users for weeks because viewModelScope.async { sync() } swallowed a SQLiteConstraintException. It only surfaced after the backend noticed stale clients.

questions.promptHtml: What does start = CoroutineStart.LAZY change compared with DEFAULT? What traps come with lazy coroutines?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lazy start looks like a harmless optimisation, but it can serialise parallel work and hang structured parents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With DEFAULT, the coroutine is scheduled on its dispatcher right away. With LAZY, it is created in the "New" state and does nothing until someone calls start(), join() or await(). The traps: if I await lazy deferreds one by one, each one starts only when awaited, so parallel work becomes sequential. A lazy child that is never started keeps its parent scope from completing, so coroutineScope hangs forever. If a lazy job is cancelled before it starts, its body never runs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Job states (more in the Job section): New (lazy only) → Active → Completing → Completed, or Cancelling → Cancelled.
  • What triggers a lazy start:
    • start() returns true if this call started it.
    • join() and await() start it implicitly and then wait.
    • awaitAll() and joinAll() start every element first.
  • A parent waits for every child to finish. A child in New never finishes on its own, so coroutineScope { async(start = LAZY) { } } never returns. Cancelling the parent does cancel the lazy child, and then the parent can complete.
  • DEFAULT with a body that was cancelled before dispatch: the body never runs. That is the cancellable-start guarantee shared by DEFAULT and LAZY.
LAZY + sequential awaits:   a ===  |  b ===  |  c ===     total = a+b+c
LAZY + awaitAll / start():  a ===
                            b ===
                            c ===                         total = max(a,b,c)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bug: hangs forever, lazy child never started
suspend fun broken() = coroutineScope {
    val unused = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { expensive() }
    "done"   // coroutineScope waits for 'unused' forever
}

// Legit: compute only if needed, but within a bounded scope
suspend fun maybe(needDetails: Boolean) = coroutineScope {
    val details = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { api.details() }
    if (needDetails) details.await() else { details.cancel(); null }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using LAZY "for performance" without a guaranteed start or cancel on every path.
  • deferreds.map { it.await() } over lazy deferreds, which is serial execution in disguise.
  • Expecting LAZY to behave like Kotlin lazy {} caching across scopes. It is bound to its scope's lifetime.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is LAZY + await() the same as calling the function directly? → It runs the block in a child coroutine, possibly on another dispatcher, but it is effectively sequential from the caller's point of view.
  2. How do you safely use a lazy deferred as a memoised value? → Create it in a long-lived owned scope (an app scope), and make sure that scope's lifetime matches the cache's lifetime.
  3. What happens when you call start() on an already-started job? → It returns false and does nothing else.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "lazy starts on await". The senior names the hanging-parent trap, the serial-await trap, and the rule that every lazy coroutine needs a guaranteed start or cancel on all code paths.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "prefetch only if needed" refactor added LAZY and forgot the cancel branch. The screen's loading coroutine never completed, so the spinner never hid on the path where details were not needed (about 30% of opens).

questions.promptHtml: Explain CoroutineStart.ATOMIC and CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED. When are they the right tool, and what can go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are rarely used, and knowing their exact guarantees separates people who read the library from people who copy snippets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both guarantee that the body starts even if the job is already cancelled. With DEFAULT it wouldn't. ATOMIC still dispatches normally, so the body is guaranteed to run eventually on the target dispatcher. Its classic use is a try/finally that must release something acquired before the launch. UNDISPATCHED runs the body right away on the caller's thread until the first real suspension point, then resumes on the coroutine's own dispatcher. I use it when code must run synchronously before launch returns, for example subscribing to a hot source before emitting into it. Its traps: that first segment ignores the dispatcher you passed, and deep nesting of undispatched coroutines can overflow the stack.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• start only governs behaviour up to the moment the body begins. After that, cancellation and dispatching are decided by the suspend calls the body makes.
  • ATOMIC:
    • Status: it was @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi for years. It was changed to @DelicateCoroutinesApi in kotlinx.coroutines 1.9.0 (#4169).
    • The body is entered, sees isActive == false, and the first suspension (for example delay) throws CancellationException.
    • Main risk: the body runs although the scope is cancelled, so it may touch resources that are no longer valid. The official docs give the example of updating UI after an Android lifecycle scope was cancelled.
  • UNDISPATCHED:
    • The body starts synchronously, before the builder returns, on the current thread. It does so even if the job is already cancelled, which the docs describe as "similar to ATOMIC".
    • The new context's elements (Job, CoroutineName) are already in place, but the thread is the caller's, even if the context says Dispatchers.IO.
    • Nested UNDISPATCHED coroutines do not form an event loop, unlike Dispatchers.Unconfined and Main.immediate. So recursion like async(start = UNDISPATCHED) { f(n-1).await() } grows the stack linearly. The docs show this with a factorial example.
  • 1.9.0 rewrote the CoroutineStart documentation (#4147). Read it for the version you ship.
Mode Dispatches first? Runs if cancelled before start? Thread of first segment
DEFAULT yes no dispatcher
LAZY on start no dispatcher
ATOMIC yes yes, until first suspension dispatcher
UNDISPATCHED no yes, until first suspension caller

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// UNDISPATCHED: guarantee subscription before we emit
val events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>()   // no replay
scope.launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) {
    events.collect { handle(it) }   // subscribed synchronously, suspends at collect
}
events.emit(Event.Ready)   // not lost

// Trap: first segment runs on the caller (Main), not IO
scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO, start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) {
    val bytes = file.readBytes()   // runs on Main, can cause jank/StrictMode violation
    upload(bytes)
}

// ATOMIC: release a lock acquired before launch even if cancelled before start
@OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)
fun CoroutineScope.releaseLater(mutex: Mutex) = launch(start = CoroutineStart.ATOMIC) {
    try { delay(100) } finally { mutex.unlock() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using UNDISPATCHED with Dispatchers.IO and blocking work before the first suspension.
  • Using ATOMIC to "make sure the work runs". It only guarantees the start, not that it completes.
  • Recursive undispatched async causing StackOverflowError under deep inputs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. UNDISPATCHED versus Dispatchers.Main.immediate? → immediate skips dispatch only when already on the right thread, and keeps doing so on every resumption, using an event loop. UNDISPATCHED applies only to the first segment, on any thread.
  2. What does viewModelScope use, and why? → Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so state updates from Main run synchronously (see the Android scopes section).
  3. Is withContext's same-dispatcher fast path undispatched? → Yes. Internally it starts the block undispatched when no switch is needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "UNDISPATCHED runs immediately". The senior gives the full start-up table, the guarantee-to-start property shared with ATOMIC, the wrong-thread trap, the stack-depth trap, and the 1.9 status change for ATOMIC.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team set UNDISPATCHED on an IO launch to "reduce latency" and introduced main-thread disk reads that StrictMode only flagged on low-end devices. The p95 frame time on a 2 GB RAM cohort doubled.

questions.promptHtml: How do you structure "fetch A and B in parallel, then combine" correctly? Why is the structured version better than starting work in an outside scope?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the canonical coroutines pattern. They are checking that you put async inside a scope that owns it, not inside GlobalScope or a captured scope.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I write a suspend function that opens coroutineScope, starts async for each independent piece, and awaits them. The function only returns when both are done. If one fails, the other is cancelled and the error is rethrown to the caller. If the caller is cancelled, both are cancelled. Starting the asyncs in GlobalScope or in an injected scope instead means a failure or cancellation does not propagate. Work leaks past the caller, and the other request keeps burning network after the screen is gone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• coroutineScope creates the parent for the children:
    • Caller cancelled → scope cancelled → children cancelled.
    • A child fails → scope cancels the siblings → coroutineScope rethrows.
    • coroutineScope returns only after all children are done.
  • Without that structure (for example GlobalScope.async inside a suspend fun):
    • Caller cancelled → nothing happens to the deferreds. They run to completion and their result is lost.
    • The first await throws → the second deferred keeps running, an orphan.
  • Concurrency versus parallelism: async gives concurrency. The real parallelism depends on the dispatcher. Network calls via suspend Retrofit already free the thread, so there is no need to put them on IO.
caller (viewModelScope.launch)
  └── coroutineScope
        ├── async { api.a() }
        └── async { api.b() }
cancel caller ⇒ all cancelled | b fails ⇒ a cancelled, error ⇒ caller

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadScreen(id: String): Screen = coroutineScope {
    val header = async { api.header(id) }
    val items = async { api.items(id) }
    Screen(header.await(), items.await())
}

// Broken: unstructured, orphans on failure/cancel
suspend fun loadScreenBroken(id: String): Screen {
    val header = GlobalScope.async { api.header(id) }
    val items = GlobalScope.async { api.items(id) }
    return Screen(header.await(), items.await())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).async { } inside a suspend function. That is a brand-new unstructured scope every call.
  • Decomposing work that depends on each other (B needs A's id) with async. Just call them sequentially.
  • Parallelising 500 items with no concurrency limit (see A1-Q300).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if B is optional and its failure shouldn't kill A? → Use supervisorScope, or catch inside B's async and return a fallback.
  2. Do I need Dispatchers.IO for the asyncs? → Not for main-safe suspend APIs. Use it for blocking SDKs.
  3. Why does coroutineScope take a lambda with CoroutineScope receiver? → So async/launch inside resolve to that scope, which is the structure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer shows two asyncs. The senior explains the three propagation directions (down for cancellation, up for failure, sibling cancellation), says when not to parallelise, and points out concurrency limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash-free but battery-heavy bug: GlobalScope.async calls kept downloading 2 MB payloads after users left the screen, which a network profiler showed as traffic with no screen visible.

questions.subtopic: async vs withContext for a single result
questions.promptHtml: A teammate writes val x = async(Dispatchers.IO) { load() }.await(). What is wrong with it, and what about val d = async { a() }; val x = b(); d.await()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can tell real overlap from ceremony. Senior engineers clean this up in review.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The first line starts a coroutine and waits for it at once. That is sequential, just slower and noisier than withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { load() }. It costs an extra Deferred, an extra child job, and a failure path that cancels the parent before await even rethrows. The second shape is legitimate: a() runs while b() runs, and we only wait when we need a's result. The rule: use async only when something useful happens between starting it and awaiting it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• async {}.await() costs one extra coroutine object, one Deferred state machine, one child registration, and possibly one dispatch. withContext creates one scoped coroutine, with no extra Deferred.
  • Error semantics differ:
    • withContext's exception is thrown straight to the caller. It also cancels the withContext scope's children.
    • async inside a regular parent cancels the parent first. So even a try/catch around await cannot recover, because the parent is already cancelling. This is the most important reason (details in the exception section).
  • Overlap pattern: start async for the long pole, do other work inline, then await.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Ceremony, plus a try/catch that does not work
suspend fun bad() = coroutineScope {
    try { async { risky() }.await() } catch (e: IOException) { fallback() }   // parent already cancelled
}

// Correct sequential with recovery
suspend fun good() = try { withContext(io) { risky() } } catch (e: IOException) { fallback() }

// Real overlap
suspend fun page(): Page = coroutineScope {
    val recs = async { api.recommendations() }   // 800 ms
    val local = repo.cached()                     // 50 ms, runs meanwhile
    Page(local, recs.await())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking async + immediate await makes code "non-blocking". withContext already is.
  • try/catch around async{}.await() inside coroutineScope to recover. The sibling and parent are already cancelling.
  • Overlapping work where the inline part is tiny. You add complexity for 5 ms.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Would the try/catch work inside supervisorScope? → Yes. The failure stays in the Deferred and is rethrown at await, where you can catch it.
  2. Is withContext cheaper if the dispatcher is the same? → Yes, it runs undispatched in place.
  3. Can a lint rule catch async{}.await()? → Yes. A simple detekt or Android Lint pattern rule can flag an async call whose only use is an immediate .await().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "both work". The senior quantifies the overhead, explains the recovery trap in non-supervisor parents, and states the "something must happen in between" rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "retry on failure" wrapper built from try { async{}.await() } never actually retried in production. The first failure cancelled the parent ViewModel coroutine, and the logs showed a JobCancellationException instead of a retry.

questions.promptHtml: If the block inside withContext finishes but the caller was cancelled at the same moment, what does withContext return? Why does that matter for resources?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a subtle guarantee (prompt cancellation) that causes real leaks of file handles, cursors and bitmaps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It returns nothing. withContext checks cancellation when it hands the result back. If the calling job was cancelled while the block ran, it throws CancellationException and the result is discarded, even though the block completed successfully. That is the prompt-cancellation guarantee, so a cancelled caller never continues. The consequence: if the block opens or creates something closeable and returns it, and cancellation races with the return, nobody owns that resource and it leaks. So I close resources inside the block, or use them inside it, and never pass them out across a withContext boundary.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The library documents withContext as cancellable on both entry and exit. On exit, when a dispatcher switch is needed, the resumption into the original context goes through cancellation-aware machinery. If the caller's job is cancelled at that point, the caller resumes with CancellationException.
  • This mirrors suspendCancellableCoroutine's prompt-cancellation guarantee, which is documented there (see the callback interop section).
  • The same family of issue is documented for withTimeout ("asynchronous timeout and resources" in the cancellation section). The pattern is the same: the value is produced, but it never reaches an owner.
Main thread                    IO thread
caller --withContext(IO)-->    block: open file, return stream
user leaves screen: cancel()   (block done, result ready)
resume on Main: job cancelled  => CancellationException; stream never closed

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Leak-prone: resource escapes the block
suspend fun openLog(): InputStream = withContext(io) { File(path).inputStream() }

// Safe: consume inside the block
suspend fun readLog(): String = withContext(io) {
    File(path).inputStream().bufferedReader().use { it.readText() }
}

// If you must hand out a resource, attach cleanup that runs on cancellation
suspend fun decode(): Bitmap {
    var bmp: Bitmap? = null
    try {
        return withContext(io) { BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path).also { bmp = it } }
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        bmp?.recycle()
        throw e
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming "the block completed, so the caller gets the value".
  • Returning Cursors, streams or large Bitmaps from withContext in code that can be cancelled.
  • Swallowing the CancellationException thrown on exit, so the code continues with no result.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does this happen when the dispatcher doesn't change? → The fast path runs in place without a dispatch back. Cancellation is still checked when the scope completes, so the safe assumption is: yes, treat any withContext exit as a cancellation point.
  2. How do you test this race? → runTest with a StandardTestDispatcher: start a withContext(other), cancel the caller after the block completes but before runCurrent() resumes it, then assert the resource was closed.
  3. Is a Room @Transaction result affected the same way? → The transaction commits, then the result may be dropped. Make the write idempotent (see the cancellation section on Room).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer doesn't know about this. The senior explains the cancellation check on exit, the leak shape, and the "consume inside, never hand out" rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gallery screen leaked file descriptors while users flicked quickly between albums. withContext(io) { contentResolver.openInputStream(uri) } results were dropped on cancellation, until the process hit the FD limit and crashed with "Too many open files".

questions.promptHtml: Explain exactly how runBlocking on the Android main thread can deadlock rather than just "be slow".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A permanent freeze is worse than an ANR-prone slowdown, and the mechanism shows whether you understand dispatchers and Loopers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: runBlocking parks the main thread until its coroutine finishes. If any code inside needs to resume on Dispatchers.Main, that resume is posted as a message to the main Looper. The Looper can't process messages because its thread is parked inside runBlocking. The coroutine waits for Main and Main waits for the coroutine, so it is a deadlock, and the ANR dialog appears after the input-dispatch timeout. Typical triggers: a repository that does withContext(Dispatchers.Main), a Flow with flowOn that collects on Main, or a library callback that posts to the main Handler.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Dispatchers.Main on Android posts to a Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).
  • runBlocking has its own event loop for coroutines dispatched to it. It does not process Looper messages.
  • Main.immediate does not dispatch if already on the main thread (isDispatchNeeded is false). So switching to it from inside runBlocking on main runs inline and does not deadlock. But a resume back from IO to Main.immediate comes from an IO thread, so it must post, and that deadlocks.
main thread: runBlocking { repo.load() }  ─── parked ───────────────────────────────▶ forever
                         └─ withContext(IO) { ... } done on IO
                         └─ withContext(Main) { notify() }  → post(msg) to main Looper
main Looper queue: [msg]  ← never drained (thread parked)
Inside runBlocking on main Result
pure suspend work on IO, no Main hop slow, blocks UI, possible ANR
withContext(Dispatchers.Main) deadlock
withContext(Main.immediate) called on main runs inline, no deadlock
IO work then resume into Main.immediate scope deadlock (the resume must post)
callback API that calls back via main Handler deadlock

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Repo(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    suspend fun token(): String {
        val t = withContext(io) { prefs.read() }
        withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { listener?.onToken(t) }   // needs Looper
        return t
    }
}

// On main thread: permanent freeze
val token = runBlocking { repo.token() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "It worked in my test." JVM unit tests have no Looper, or setMain replaces it, so the deadlock never shows.
  • Adding runBlocking(Dispatchers.IO). The main thread still parks and the Main hop is still blocked.
  • Assuming a timeout inside runBlocking fixes it. withTimeout can fire, because runBlocking's own event loop handles the delay, but only if the code hangs at a cancellable point, and it still freezes the UI for that long.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does this look in an ANR trace? → Main thread in BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking → LockSupport.parkNanos, with nothing on IO doing work.
  2. Why can't the event loop of runBlocking run the Main task? → It is a different dispatcher. Only tasks dispatched to runBlocking's own loop run there.
  3. What's the fix? → Remove runBlocking: make the caller asynchronous with lifecycleScope.launch, or restructure startup to show a placeholder and update later.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "runBlocking blocks the UI". The senior traces the Looper message dependency, spells out the Main versus Main.immediate cases, and knows what the ANR stack looks like.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A SDK started posting its init callback to the main Handler, and a runBlocking { sdk.awaitInit() } in Application.onCreate turned from "200 ms slow" into a 100% hang on that SDK version. Cold-start ANR spiked within hours of rollout.

questions.promptHtml: Why is calling runBlocking from inside a coroutine, or from a thread of Dispatchers.Default/IO, dangerous even when it's not on the main thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows understanding of bounded pools and nested blocking, which is how server and SDK code deadlocks under load.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: runBlocking parks the current worker thread, so that thread does nothing until the inner coroutine finishes. On Dispatchers.Default there are only as many threads as CPU cores, for example 8. If 8 coroutines each call runBlocking and the inner work needs a Default thread to make progress, nothing can run, and the app is in a pool-starvation deadlock. On IO the limit is 64 threads by default, so it hides longer and then fails under load. The library docs say plainly that runBlocking should not be used from a coroutine. Inside suspend code I call the suspend function directly or use withContext.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Sizes (see the dispatchers section for detail): Default = number of CPU cores (minimum 2). IO = 64 or the core count, whichever is higher, and it shares threads with Default.
  • The deadlock condition: every worker that could execute the inner coroutine is parked waiting for one.
Default pool (4 threads), 4 coroutines each do runBlocking { withContext(Default) { work() } }
T1: parked in runBlocking ─┐
T2: parked in runBlocking ─┤  inner work() queued on Default, no free thread
T3: parked in runBlocking ─┤  => no progress, ever
T4: parked in runBlocking ─┘
  • Even without a full deadlock, every parked thread lowers throughput: the effective pool size is N minus the number of blocked threads. Latency climbs as nonlinear queueing.
  • Some libraries hide runBlocking inside synchronous APIs, for example a blocking "get" wrapper around a suspend cache. Calling those from coroutines re-creates the problem one level down.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Blocking API wrapping suspend code
class Cache { fun getBlocking(k: String) = runBlocking { get(k) }; suspend fun get(k: String): V = TODO() }

// Called from coroutines on Default — starvation under load
suspend fun process(keys: List<String>) = coroutineScope {
    keys.map { async(Dispatchers.Default) { cache.getBlocking(it) } }.awaitAll()
}

// Fix: stay in suspend world
suspend fun processFixed(keys: List<String>) = coroutineScope {
    keys.map { async { cache.get(it) } }.awaitAll()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking "it's on a background thread, so blocking is fine". The pool is finite and shared.
  • Moving the call to IO to "fix" starvation. It only raises the ceiling to 64 and still caps throughput.
  • Using a runBlocking bridge in an OkHttp interceptor that itself waits on another OkHttp call, which is two-level pool coupling (see the cross-cutting scenarios).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you see this in production? → Thread dumps or Perfetto: all DefaultDispatcher-worker-* threads in parkNanos under runBlocking. Coroutine debug dumps show the inner coroutines stuck in the queue.
  2. Is runBlocking OK in a WorkManager Worker.doWork()? → It works (a background executor thread, bounded by the job), but CoroutineWorker is the idiomatic choice (see the Android scopes section).
  3. When is a blocking bridge unavoidable, and how do you make it safe? → A synchronous framework callback such as OkHttp Authenticator. Use runBlocking with a bounded withTimeout, make sure the inner work never needs the same pool or lock, and dedupe concurrent callers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "don't use runBlocking". The senior quantifies the pool sizes, describes the starvation-deadlock condition, recognises hidden runBlocking in libraries, and gives safe-bridge rules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync engine processed batches with async(Default), each calling a "blocking" key-store wrapper that used runBlocking inside. It ran fine on 8-core test phones and deadlocked on 4-core budget devices once batches exceeded 4 items.

questions.promptHtml: When should a function be suspend fun and when should it be an extension on CoroutineScope? Why is suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo() a smell?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: API design across a team decides whether structured concurrency holds. This convention comes from the coroutines library authors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A suspend fun does its work and returns when the work is done. It may use coroutineScope for internal parallelism, but nothing outlives the call. A function with a CoroutineScope receiver, like launch and async, starts work and returns right away, and the work continues in the caller's scope. Those are two different contracts. Combining them, suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo(), is ambiguous. Inside it, launch resolves to the receiver scope rather than to the suspend call's own context, so work can escape the "this function finishes before returning" promise. Pick one: suspend and wait, or scope extension and fire.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The two contracts:
    • suspend fun load(): Data means "when I return, everything I started is done." Internally: coroutineScope { async…; async… }.
    • fun CoroutineScope.startPolling(): Job means "I start something in your scope and return at once." The caller owns the lifetime.
  • The smell: in suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo(), a bare launch {} uses the receiver's coroutineContext, but kotlin.coroutines.coroutineContext (the suspend function's own context) could be different. The IDE warns about this ambiguity. Reviewers get confused, and work escapes the caller's wait.
  • Class-level scopes: a repository that injects an externalScope (an app scope) to run work that must survive the caller follows the same idea. Only methods that state "fire and continue" use it.
  • Naming: functions that launch should read like it, for example startX, launchX, xIn(scope), mirroring launchIn and stateIn(scope).
Signature Returns when Lifetime owner
suspend fun f(): T work done the call
fun CoroutineScope.f(): Job immediately caller's scope
suspend fun CoroutineScope.f() ambiguous unclear, avoid

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Good: waits
suspend fun syncAll() = coroutineScope {
    launch { syncContacts() }
    launch { syncMessages() }
}   // returns after both

// Good: fires into caller's scope
fun CoroutineScope.startHeartbeat(period: Long): Job = launch {
    while (isActive) { ping(); delay(period) }
}

// Smell: which context does launch use? Does syncAllSmell() wait?
suspend fun CoroutineScope.syncAllSmell() {
    launch { syncContacts() }   // goes into receiver scope; caller returns before it finishes
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing viewModelScope into repositories as a parameter so they can launch. The repository then controls the lifetime of ViewModel work.
  • Returning Job/Deferred from suspend functions.
  • Using coroutineContext inside a scope-receiver suspend fun and getting the wrong Job.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A repository must write analytics that survives screen exit. What signature? → fun log(e: Event) that launches into an injected app scope, or a suspend fun that does externalScope.launch { }.join() so the caller waits but the work cannot be cancelled by the caller.
  2. Why do launchIn(scope) and stateIn(scope, …) take the scope as an argument? → They make the "starts work in your scope" contract explicit at the call site.
  3. How do you enforce the convention? → Review checklist plus a detekt rule flagging suspend fun CoroutineScope. declarations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "suspend for suspending work". The senior states the two contracts, explains the receiver-context ambiguity, and connects it to how scope ownership is designed across layers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "suspend fun CoroutineScope.refresh()" helper made pull-to-refresh hide its spinner before the refresh finished, because the launches went into the receiver scope. Ops then saw duplicate refreshes from users pulling again.

questions.subtopic: Sharing a Deferred for in-flight deduplication
questions.promptHtml: Three screens request the same config at once. How would you use async/Deferred to make one network call and share the result, and what are the pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a builder applied to a real design problem, and the bugs here (shared cancellation, cached failure) are subtle.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I keep a map from key to Deferred. The first caller creates the deferred with async in a long-lived scope I own (an app scope), not in its own scope, then everyone await()s the same instance. Because the deferred's owner is the app scope, one caller cancelling only stops that caller's wait, not the request. When the deferred completes I remove it from the map, so a failure isn't cached forever and later calls refresh. Map access is guarded, and nothing suspends while holding the guard.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why not create the deferred in the caller's scope: if screen A starts it in A's viewModelScope and A is closed, the deferred is cancelled, and screens B and C waiting on it get CancellationException for no reason.
  • await() cancellation is per waiter (A1-Q279), so waiters can come and go.
  • Failure caching: a completed-exceptionally Deferred rethrows forever. Remove it from the map in invokeOnCompletion, and keep the value in a proper cache instead.
  • Races: "check map, then insert" must be atomic. Use synchronized (fine, no suspension inside), ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent, or a Mutex (see the shared-state section).
  • CoroutineStart.LAZY + computeIfAbsent: create the deferred lazily inside computeIfAbsent (which may call the lambda more than once on contention in some implementations, so lazy creation prevents duplicate starts), then start() it outside.
  • Should the request be cancelled if all waiters leave? This trade-off needs a reference count. Usually it's simpler to let it finish and warm the cache.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ConfigLoader(private val appScope: CoroutineScope, private val api: Api) {
    private val inFlight = HashMap<String, Deferred<Config>>()

    suspend fun load(key: String): Config {
        val d = synchronized(inFlight) {
            inFlight.getOrPut(key) {
                appScope.async { api.config(key) }.also { def ->
                    def.invokeOnCompletion { synchronized(inFlight) { inFlight.remove(key) } }
                }
            }
        }
        return d.await()   // caller cancellation cancels only this await
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• async in the caller's scope, so one screen closing kills the call for every screen.
  • Never removing completed deferreds, so a transient error is cached forever.
  • Calling await() inside the synchronized block, which blocks other callers and can deadlock.
  • appScope without a SupervisorJob: one failed request cancels the app scope and every future request fails at once.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why must appScope use SupervisorJob? → With a plain Job, the first failing async cancels the whole scope permanently, and every later async in it is cancelled at birth.
  2. Could invokeOnCompletion remove a newer deferred for the same key? → Only if a new one was inserted before removal. Guard with if (inFlight[key] === def) remove.
  3. How would you test this? → runTest, a fake API that suspends on a CompletableDeferred, three concurrent load calls, assert one API call. Then cancel one caller and assert the other two still get the value.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer suggests "cache the result". The senior shares the in-flight deferred under the right owner, handles removal and failure, notes the need for SupervisorJob, and keeps suspension out of critical sections.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cold start fired 6 identical /config calls from different modules. Deduplication via a shared deferred cut startup network bytes by about 5x, and fixed a rate-limit 429 the backend was returning to multi-module clients.

questions.contextHtml:
A product page should load in roughly the time of its slowest call. Each of the 4 calls takes 300–500 ms on p50. QA measures about 1.6 s for the page on Wi-Fi and asks why "the async version" is not faster than the old sequential code.

suspend fun loadProduct(id: String): Product = coroutineScope {
    val parts = listOf("info", "price", "stock", "reviews")
        .map { part -> async { api.part(id, part) }.await() }
    Product.from(parts)
}

A teammate suggests the dispatcher is the problem and wants to add Dispatchers.IO.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Dispatchers.IO to the async calls", or "Retrofit is slow." Neither changes anything. The code awaits each deferred inside map before starting the next one.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the 4 calls independent? (Yes, so parallel is valid.) Is api.part a Retrofit suspend function? (Yes, so it's already main-safe and IO is a red herring.) Should one failure fail the whole page? (It decides whether to use coroutineScope or supervisorScope.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. Fix in the next build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Sequential awaits inside map: every iteration starts one async and waits for it at once. (b) An OkHttp per-host connection limit: maxRequestsPerHost defaults to 5, so it doesn't matter for 4 calls. (c) A dispatcher issue: not relevant, because suspend Retrofit doesn't block a thread.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add timestamps around each call in logs, or use the network profiler. The calls start one after another (start of call n+1 = end of call n). After the fix, they start within a millisecond of each other.
  5. Root cause: map { async { }.await() } builds no overlap. Total ≈ 400 + 400 + 400 + 400 ≈ 1.6 s at a 400 ms average. That matches QA.
  6. Fix:
suspend fun loadProduct(id: String): Product = coroutineScope {
    val parts = listOf("info", "price", "stock", "reviews")
        .map { part -> async { api.part(id, part) } }   // start all
        .awaitAll()                                       // then wait
    Product.from(parts)
}

Expected time ≈ max(300..500) ≈ 500 ms plus a little overhead, about a 3x improvement. 7. Prevention: A lint rule for async { … }.await() in the same expression. A benchmark or macrobenchmark on page load. Code-review note: "start all, then await". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not add Dispatchers.IO. It adds a context switch and fixes nothing. I would not go with GlobalScope "to make them independent", which loses structure.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reviews can fail without breaking the page? → Wrap that one async body in a try/catch that returns an empty result, or use supervisorScope with per-item runCatching (re-throw CancellationException).
  • What if there were 400 parts? → Bound the concurrency (see A1-Q300).
  • Does awaitAll keep the order? → Yes, the results follow the input order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: In one codebase, a "parallelise everything" PR added async everywhere using exactly this shape and measured no gain. It was nearly reverted as "coroutines don't help". A two-line move of .await() brought the 3x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the dispatcher or the network, or doesn't see the inline await.
  • Hire: spots the sequential await and fixes it with start-then-awaitAll.
  • Strong hire: also computes the expected latency, dismisses the IO red herring with a reason, and discusses failure policy and concurrency bounds.

questions.contextHtml: A banking dashboard (1.2M DAU, 60% of devices are mid- or low-end Android 10–13) shows 5 widgets on open: balance (p50 250 ms / p95 900 ms), transactions (400 / 1,400), offers (600 / 2,500), credit score (300 / 1,100), notifications (150 / 500). The current ViewModel calls them one after another and shows a full-screen spinner until all are done. The product team wants "dashboard visible under 1 s at p95". Today the p95 time-to-content is about 5.8 s. The offers service is owned by another team and has a known 2–3% error rate.
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure the loading with coroutine builders, and what numbers do you expect?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap all five in async and awaitAll." That fixes the sum but makes p95 equal the slowest service's p95 (offers, 2.5 s). The 3% offers error rate then blanks the whole dashboard under fail-fast.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which widgets are critical to show the screen? Probably balance and transactions. Is partial rendering OK? Are there caches (Room) that can render immediately? Is there a backend aggregation endpoint (BFF) option? Do any calls depend on each other (the credit score needing a customer id from balance)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag the new loader at 5%, and compare p95 time-to-content and error rate against the control group.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Sequential calls: sum of p50s = 250 + 400 + 600 + 300 + 150 = 1,700 ms. The p95s don't add exactly, but the sum is about 6.4 s and the observed value is 5.8 s, which is consistent.
    • (b) All-or-nothing gating: the slowest and least reliable service gates everything.
    • (c) Main-thread work: probably not the bottleneck. Verify with a trace.
  4. How I'd verify each: Custom trace sections or a Firebase Performance trace per call. A Perfetto trace of the open shows long idle gaps on Main, which means waiting, not computing. Crashlytics or analytics for the error rate per widget.
  5. Root cause: Sequential awaits plus a single combined UI state.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: render each widget independently in supervisorScope, as per-widget state. The critical path is only balance + transactions, with p95 ≈ max(900, 1,400) = 1.4 s. To get under 1 s, show Room-cached values instantly and refresh in the background.
private fun loadDashboard() = viewModelScope.launch {
    supervisorScope {
        launch { load(Widget.BALANCE) { api.balance() } }
        launch { load(Widget.TRANSACTIONS) { api.transactions() } }
        launch { load(Widget.OFFERS) { withTimeout(1_500) { api.offers() } } }
        launch { load(Widget.SCORE) { api.score() } }
        launch { load(Widget.NOTIFS) { api.notifications() } }
    }
}

private suspend fun <T> load(w: Widget, block: suspend () -> T) {
    _state.update { it.with(w, WidgetState.Loading) }
    val result = try { WidgetState.Data(block()) }
                 catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }   // includes TimeoutCancellationException
                 catch (e: Exception) { WidgetState.Error }
    _state.update { it.with(w, result) }
}
  • Note: withTimeout's TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, so the code above re-throws it. If I want a timeout to mean "error tile", I use withTimeoutOrNull and map null to Error (see the cancellation section).
  • Long-term: a BFF aggregate endpoint for the critical widgets, plus cache-first rendering.
  1. Prevention: p95 time-to-first-widget and time-to-critical-content dashboards. A per-widget error-rate SLO. A macrobenchmark in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not awaitAll everything, which is fail-fast and gated by the slowest service. I would not catch Exception without re-throwing cancellation. I would not put launch children in supervisorScope without per-child try/catch, because a failure would go to the uncaught handler and crash. The parallel fan-out does raise peak concurrent requests from 1 to 5 per open: check backend capacity and OkHttp's maxRequestsPerHost (default 5).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Credit score needs the customer id from balance? → Chain inside one child: launch { val b = api.balance(); score(b.customerId) }. Keep the other children parallel.
  • The user pulls to refresh while loading? → Keep the Job, and cancel and restart, or ignore while active (see the shared-state section on duplicate actions).
  • Why does each _state.update need the atomic update {}? → Five children write concurrently. On Main.immediate they interleave only at suspension points, but update is still the safe, dispatcher-independent choice.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team went straight to awaitAll, celebrated the p50 drop, then saw "dashboard error" complaints triple. The 3% offers failures had become 3% blank dashboards. Per-widget supervision fixed it within a release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps it sequential or doesn't know how to parallelise.
  • Hire: parallelises with async/launch and computes the new latency.
  • Strong hire: separates the critical path from optional widgets, uses supervisorScope with per-child error handling, gets the TimeoutCancellationException subtlety right, and weighs backend load and caching.

questions.contextHtml:
After a release, a news app (800k DAU) sees: no crash increase, but backend traffic to /article/related up 2.4x, battery complaints in reviews, and LeakCanary reports in internal builds about ArticleFragment retained via a lambda. The relevant new code:

class ArticleViewModel(private val api: Api) : ViewModel() {
    private var related: Deferred<List<Article>>? = null
    fun open(id: String) {
        related = GlobalScope.async(Dispatchers.IO) { api.related(id) }
    }
    suspend fun relatedArticles() = related?.await().orEmpty()
}
// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    adapter.submit(vm.relatedArticles()); binding.relatedHeader.isVisible = true
}

Users swipe between articles quickly, about 7 articles a minute.
questions.promptHtml: Explain every symptom, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "GlobalScope is bad, use viewModelScope." It's correct but incomplete. It doesn't explain the 2.4x traffic, the silent failures, or the leak path.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is open() called on every pager page change, including pre-loaded offscreen pages? Does api.related retry? Which object exactly does LeakCanary say holds the Fragment? Do we have an analytics counter for "related shown"?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A server-side cache or rate limit for /article/related. Remote-config to disable related prefetch if a flag exists. Ship a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Every open() starts an unowned request. Swiping or ViewPager pre-loading calls open for neighbours, and nothing cancels the old ones when the ViewModel clears, so requests keep running. This is the 2.4x traffic and battery cost.
    • (b) Failures are silent: GlobalScope.async with no awaiter or a lost awaiter stores the exception and never reports it, so no crash appears.
    • (c) The leak is the Fragment's coroutine closure (binding) waiting on a long-running await. But viewLifecycleOwner cancels it at view destroy, so that is a red herring unless the waiting coroutine is in a wider scope. Check LeakCanary's actual path: it may be the ViewModel captured by a long-lived GlobalScope lambda (holding api, and the ViewModel via this).
  4. How I'd verify each: The network profiler during fast swiping shows requests continuing after leaving. Add CoroutineName("related-$id") plus the debug probes dump (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()) in a debug build to list live GlobalScope coroutines. The LeakCanary trace shows a reference chain through DispatchedContinuation or the coroutine's lambda.
  5. Root cause: GlobalScope has no Job. The deferred is not a child of anything, so ViewModel clearing doesn't cancel it, failures are only stored, and the lambda captures the ViewModel (implicit this for api) for as long as the request runs, including retries and timeouts of 30 s+. The field is also overwritten each time, so old deferreds are orphaned.
  6. Fix:
class ArticleViewModel(private val api: Api) : ViewModel() {
    private val _related = MutableStateFlow<List<Article>>(emptyList())
    val related: StateFlow<List<Article>> = _related.asStateFlow()
    private var loadJob: Job? = null

    fun open(id: String) {
        loadJob?.cancel()
        loadJob = viewModelScope.launch {
            _related.value = try { api.related(id) }
                catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
                catch (e: IOException) { emptyList() }
        }
    }
}

The Fragment collects related with repeatOnLifecycle (see the Flow lifecycle section). This is short-term. Long-term, move to a repository with a cache. 7. Prevention: GlobalScope is @DelicateCoroutinesApi (since 1.5), so make the opt-in a lint error. A detekt rule GlobalCoroutineUsage. Review the checklist item "who cancels this?". Network-volume alerts per endpoint. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not swap to CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) created per ViewModel without cancelling it in onCleared. That is the same bug with a different name. I would not keep exposing a Deferred to the UI, which is a public API leaking concurrency internals.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should prefetch survive a fast swipe? → Only if the cache is shared: run it through an app-scoped dedupe (A1-Q293), with cancellation when the page is far away.
  • Why no crash at all? → async with a missing or cancelled waiter keeps its exception. GlobalScope has no parent to cancel.
  • Would viewModelScope.async be enough? → It fixes the lifetime, but failures are still silent if not awaited. A state-based launch is cleaner.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless prefetch" with GlobalScope.async doubled API spend for an endpoint behind a paid third-party data provider before anyone noticed. Finance found it before engineering did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "replace GlobalScope", nothing more, or blames Retrofit.
  • Hire: explains the missing parent → no cancellation → extra traffic, and moves to viewModelScope with job replacement.
  • Strong hire: explains the silent failures and the leak via the captured ViewModel, separates the red herring in the Fragment scope, verifies with the debug probes and network profiler, and adds a lint gate.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout screen's "Place order" button stays in loading state forever for about 30% of users (those without a coupon). No crash, no error log. The spinner is cleared in the line after coroutineScope returns.

suspend fun prepareCheckout(cart: Cart): Summary = coroutineScope {
    val coupon = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { api.validateCoupon(cart.couponCode!!) }
    val totals = async { api.totals(cart) }
    val discount = if (cart.couponCode != null) coupon.await().amount else 0
    Summary(totals.await(), discount)
}

A teammate suspects the !! causes a hidden NPE and wants to add logging around api.totals.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it hang, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
