sections.html: "The !! throws an NPE." It doesn't: the lazy body never runs on the no-coupon path. Or "totals is slow", which is a red herring because totals completes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it reproduce only without a coupon? (Yes, 30%.) Does totals return? (Logs say yes.) Is there a timeout on the screen? (No.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: A server-side or remote flag can't fix client code. Hotfix release. Meanwhile, set the support script to "add any coupon" as a workaround, if acceptable.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) An unstarted LAZY child keeps coroutineScope from completing. When there's no coupon, coupon is never started, so the scope waits forever.
    • (b) The !! NPE: it would only throw if the body ran. It doesn't, so this is not the cause.
    • (c) A network hang in totals: ruled out by the logs.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with runTest and a fake API. The no-coupon case times out (runTest's default timeout fails the test). DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() shows the coupon coroutine in state CREATED (lazy, not started) and the parent waiting for children.
  5. Root cause: coroutineScope returns only after all children complete. A LAZY child in the New state never completes unless it is started or cancelled. The code body returns Summary, but the scope is still "completing", waiting on coupon.
  6. Fix: Don't create work you might not need:
suspend fun prepareCheckout(cart: Cart): Summary = coroutineScope {
    val code = cart.couponCode
    val coupon = code?.let { async { api.validateCoupon(it) } }   // only if needed, eager
    val totals = async { api.totals(cart) }
    Summary(totals.await(), coupon?.await()?.amount ?: 0)
}

Or, if LAZY is truly required: else { coupon.cancel(); 0 } on every branch. 7. Prevention: A unit test for each branch. A rule against CoroutineStart.LAZY without a documented start/cancel path. Screen-level timeouts and an analytics event when the spinner is shown for more than 10 s. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not add withTimeout around the whole thing as "the fix". It hides the bug and turns it into a 10 s error. I would not switch to GlobalScope so the scope "doesn't wait", which leaks the work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would supervisorScope change anything? → No. It also waits for all children.
  • Is there a hang if the user leaves the screen? → No. Cancelling the parent cancels the lazy child, so the scope completes as cancelled.
  • Would awaitAll(coupon, totals) have hidden the bug? → It would start coupon and then throw an NPE from !! on the no-coupon path. A different bug, but at least it's visible.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "micro-optimisation" PR made a coupon check lazy to save one request. In production it froze checkout for every guest user. The conversion-funnel alert caught it before any crash tool did.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the !! or the network.
  • Hire: identifies the unstarted lazy child blocking coroutineScope and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: explains the Job state (New) and the parent-completion rule, proves it with a test or debug dump, and generalises it into a team rule.

questions.contextHtml:
A travel app's search results page fetches flights, hotels and cars in parallel. Product wants "show whatever succeeded". After release, the following is observed. When the cars API returns 503 (about 4% of requests), the page shows flights and hotels correctly, which is good. But when users leave the page mid-load, Crashlytics shows no crash, yet the leaving users' next screen sometimes freezes on a spinner. Also, a coroutine-timeout bug report: "pressing back during search doesn't stop the network calls".

suspend fun search(q: Query): SearchResult = supervisorScope {
    val flights = async { api.flights(q) }
    val hotels = async { api.hotels(q) }
    val cars = async { api.cars(q) }
    SearchResult(
        flights = runCatching { flights.await() }.getOrNull(),
        hotels = runCatching { hotels.await() }.getOrNull(),
        cars = runCatching { cars.await() }.getOrNull(),
    )
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with this code, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, supervisorScope gives partial results." It misses that runCatching catches CancellationException.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this called from viewModelScope? Is the screen cancelled when the user presses back? (yes, viewModelScope is cleared). Does any caller rely on the function throwing when cancelled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix release. No server-side lever.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) runCatching { await() } swallows CancellationException, so a cancelled caller doesn't stop: the function returns a SearchResult of all nulls and the caller proceeds as if it were a real "no results" outcome. (b) The empty result gets cached or rendered, which causes the stuck spinner or a wrong "no results" state. (c) The "network calls don't stop" claim: await() in a cancelled coroutine throws, but the async children are cancelled by the cancelled supervisorScope, so the calls do stop. This is partly a red herring. Verify with the network profiler.
  4. How I'd verify each: A runTest test: start search, cancel the job, and assert that it ends cancelled (job.isCancelled) and does not produce a result. Log the thread and result at the call site.
  5. Root cause: runCatching catches Throwable, including CancellationException. Cancellation is cooperative signalling via that exception (see the cancellation section). Swallowing it makes the cancelled function "complete normally" with garbage. The structure is right (supervisor for independence), but failure handling is wrong. A related point: supervisorScope does not make async failures harmless, it just leaves them in the Deferred until awaited.
  6. Fix:
private suspend fun <T> Deferred<T>.awaitOrNull(): T? =
    try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { null }

suspend fun search(q: Query): SearchResult = supervisorScope {
    val flights = async { api.flights(q) }
    val hotels = async { api.hotels(q) }
    val cars = async { api.cars(q) }
    SearchResult(flights.awaitOrNull(), hotels.awaitOrNull(), cars.awaitOrNull())
}

Caveat: if the caller itself was not cancelled but cars was cancelled for an unrelated reason (its own withTimeout throwing TimeoutCancellationException), the helper above rethrows it and kills the whole result. For per-call timeouts, use withTimeoutOrNull inside the async body and keep the awaitOrNull helper for real failures. Also check ensureActive() after the awaits if I want to be strict. 7. Prevention: detekt rule for runCatching around suspend calls (a lint like SuspendFunWithCoroutineScopeReceiver is not it, the right check is "runCatching with suspend call"). A test for the cancelled path in every parallel loader. Review checklist: "does any catch-all rethrow CancellationException?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not catch Throwable. I would not model per-source errors as null: a sealed SourceResult.Success/Failure lets the UI show "cars unavailable" instead of silently hiding the row.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not make each async body catch its own exceptions? → That also works and avoids the helper: async { try { api.cars(q) } catch (e: IOException) { null } }. Catching a narrow exception type also avoids swallowing cancellation.
  • Is getOrNull() on Result the problem? → No. The problem is what got caught.
  • Would the freeze vanish if the UI treated all-null as an error? → It would mask the symptom. The function must stay cancellable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A catch-all runCatching in a shared helper turned every cancelled search into an empty result written to a local cache. Users later saw "no flights" until the cache expired. The helper was in 14 call sites.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves the code as is.
  • Hire: spots that runCatching swallows cancellation and rethrows it.
  • Strong hire: explains the supervisor semantics, handles the timeout-versus-caller-cancellation subtlety, and proposes typed per-source results and a lint rule.

questions.contextHtml:
A chat app (2M DAU) has a SharedFlow<Message> (replay = 0) in a repository, fed by a WebSocket. In ChatViewModel.init the team launches a collector and then immediately asks the repository to request "history sync", which makes the server push the last messages through the same socket. About 1 in 150 opens loses the first few messages: the list is missing the newest message until the next one arrives. It only happens on fast devices and fast networks. A teammate proposes delay(50) between the collect and the sync request. Another proposes replay = 1.

init {
    viewModelScope.launch { repo.messages.collect { append(it) } }
    repo.requestHistorySync()   // server pushes messages immediately
}
questions.promptHtml: Why are messages lost, and what is the right fix? Discuss at least three options.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a delay", or "use replay", without understanding that the collector subscription happens late, because launch is dispatched.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is requestHistorySync blocking, or does it only enqueue a request? Is history also persisted (DB), so the UI could read from there? Does ordering matter? Can messages arrive twice?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by option B below (small, safe). Ship behind a flag, watch the "missing newest message" support tickets.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The collector is not subscribed yet: viewModelScope.launch uses Main.immediate, so it runs inline when init is on the main thread, which is often true. But if the ViewModel is created on another thread (for example via a background pre-creation), or the launch is queued behind a pending dispatch, the body runs later. The first emit then has zero subscribers and is dropped by a replay = 0 flow. (b) The server push races the subscription on fast devices. (c) A UI-layer bug. Less likely, since only the first messages are lost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log timestamps at "collect started" versus "first emit". A test with StandardTestDispatcher: the launch isn't run until runCurrent(), and the emission happens before it, which reproduces the loss deterministically. Check subscriptionCount at emit time.
  5. Root cause: A SharedFlow with no replay drops values emitted while there are no subscribers. launch with the default start schedules the body; the code that follows (requestHistorySync) can run before the body starts collecting. There is no happens-before between "subscribed" and "request sent".
  6. Fix options:
    • A. delay(50): wrong. It is a timing guess and fails on a slow device.
    • B. Start the collector with CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED: the body runs synchronously up to its first suspension, which is collect registering the subscriber. Then the request is sent safely.
init {
    viewModelScope.launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) {
        repo.messages.collect { append(it) }   // subscribes before launch returns
    }
    repo.requestHistorySync()
}
  • C. replay = N: hides the race by caching, but the semantics change: late collectors replay stale messages (duplicates after a configuration change, for example).
  • D. Best long-term: make the database the source of truth. The socket writes to Room, the UI collects dao.observeMessages(), which emits the current state on collection, so there is no race at all. I'd ship B as the hotfix and plan D.
  1. Prevention: a test with a StandardTestDispatcher that verifies the subscription before the request (runCurrent() order). Wait for subscriptionCount in tests. A design rule: never rely on "collector started before producer" without a guarantee.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not use delay. I would not use Channel.UNLIMITED to buffer all pushes into the ViewModel: it hides ordering and memory issues. UNDISPATCHED's caveat: the first segment runs on the caller's thread, and the first segment here is just the subscription, so it is safe. If the first segment did heavy work, it would block.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not onSubscription { requestHistorySync() }? → Good option for SharedFlow: messages.onSubscription { repo.requestHistorySync() }.collect {}. It runs after the subscription is registered, so nothing is lost, and it is arguably the cleanest in-flow answer.
  • What about Main.immediate, does it already do this? → Only if the launch happens on the main thread, and only until the first real suspension. It is not a guarantee on other threads.
  • ATOMIC here? → No. It still dispatches, so the race remains.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments-status screen was missing its "success" event once in a few hundred runs. The root cause was identical: a hot flow with no replay and a launch that had not yet subscribed. The permanent fix was to persist the state and observe it, not to tune start modes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a delay, or can't explain why values are dropped.
  • Hire: explains the subscription race and uses UNDISPATCHED or onSubscription.
  • Strong hire: compares the options (delay, replay, UNDISPATCHED, onSubscription, DB as source of truth), knows the thread caveat of the first segment, and writes a deterministic test.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-backup feature calls api.checkExists(hash) for every local photo before upload. In beta (users with about 300 photos) it was fine. The launch cohort has users with 15,000 photos on 3 GB RAM devices. The code:

suspend fun missing(photos: List<Photo>): List<Photo> = coroutineScope {
    photos.map { p -> async { p to api.checkExists(p.hash) } }
        .awaitAll()
        .filter { !it.second }
        .map { it.first }
}

Symptoms: the server returns many 429s; OkHttp logs show IOException: Canceled/timeouts; Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError in 0.8% of sessions; the whole feature fails when one call returns 500 (about 1 in 3,000 calls fails, so with 15,000 calls nearly every run fails).
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong at 15,000 items, and how do you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Dispatchers.IO", or "chunk the list into 100". Chunking helps memory but not fail-fast, and the dispatcher isn't the limit for suspend network calls.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a batch endpoint (checkExistsBatch(hashes))? What is the server's rate limit? Must the result be all-or-nothing? Can the work resume after a process death?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A remote flag to cap the library size per run. A server-side rate limit is already hitting back, so lower the client concurrency first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 15,000 coroutines + 15,000 Deferreds + 15,000 Pairs live at once. Coroutines are cheap (roughly a few hundred bytes each), so memory is about a few MB, not the OOM cause by itself. But 15,000 queued OkHttp Calls, request objects and response buffers are heavier. OkHttp's dispatcher runs maxRequests = 64 and maxRequestsPerHost = 5 and queues the rest. (b) Timeouts are counted from the call start for queued calls in some setups, so queued calls time out while waiting. (c) Fail-fast: with a 1-in-3,000 failure, the chance that at least one of 15,000 calls fails is 1 − (1 − 1/3000)^15000 ≈ 1 − e^−5 ≈ 99.3%, so nearly every run fails. (d) Dispatchers: a red herring for suspend calls.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump in the Android Studio memory profiler at peak. The OkHttp EventListener queue time per call. Server dashboards for 429 per client. Count live coroutines with the debug probes in a debug build.
  5. Root cause: Unbounded fan-out. Concurrency should be a chosen number, not equal to the input size. And all-or-nothing failure semantics don't suit an N-item batch where each item is independent.
  6. Fix:
suspend fun missing(photos: List<Photo>): List<Photo> {
    val gate = Semaphore(permits = 8)
    return supervisorScope {
        photos.map { p ->
            async {
                gate.withPermit {
                    try { p to !api.checkExists(p.hash) }
                    catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
                    catch (e: IOException) { p to false }   // unknown: retry later, don't fail the run
                }
            }
        }.awaitAll().filter { it.second }.map { it.first }
    }
}

The permit limits real work, but 15,000 async objects still exist. For true bounding, process through a pipeline: photos.asFlow().flatMapMerge(concurrency = 8) { flow { emit(...) } } (see the operators section), or a fixed set of 8 workers reading from a Channel. Best of all: a batch endpoint with 200 hashes per request, which reduces calls by 200x. 7. Prevention: a load test with a 20k-item fixture. A metric: peak concurrent in-flight requests. A review rule: "every fan-out has a bound". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not set the concurrency equal to the CPU count: these calls are I/O, so 8 to 16 depends on the server limit and radio, not cores. I would not raise maxRequestsPerHost to "go faster". I would not make the whole run fail on one error, but I would track the failed items for a retry pass.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does the semaphore not fix memory? → The coroutines and deferreds are still allocated up front. Only the active work is bounded. Use a flow with flatMapMerge or worker coroutines to bound objects too.
  • Would limitedParallelism(8) work instead? → It limits threads of a dispatcher, not suspended calls: all 15,000 suspended requests can still be in flight. It bounds blocking work, not suspending concurrency.
  • User kills the app mid-run? → Persist progress (checked hashes) in Room, and make the job resumable by WorkManager.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration to coroutines removed an implicit thread-pool bound the old Executor code had, and the backend's rate limiter lit up the day the feature went wide. The fix was a one-line permit count, and a dashboard graph named "client concurrency".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes it with a dispatcher change, or doesn't see the unbounded fan-out.
  • Hire: bounds the concurrency with a semaphore or chunking and handles per-item failure.
  • Strong hire: does the failure-probability math, separates object count from active-work bound, prefers a batch API and a flow-based or worker-pool design, and plans resumability.

questions.contextHtml:
A "Place order" function should respond to the user as soon as the order is confirmed. Analytics and a push-registration refresh are "nice to have". The developer wrote:

suspend fun placeOrder(cart: Cart): Order = coroutineScope {
    val order = api.placeOrder(cart)           // p50 400 ms
    launch { analytics.track(order) }          // p50 150 ms, p95 6 s (third-party SDK)
    launch { push.refreshRegistration() }      // p50 300 ms
    order
}

Users on slow networks complain the confirmation screen appears "late", and the p95 of "tap to confirmation" is 6.6 s although the order endpoint's p95 is 900 ms. QA says "the function returns order on the last line, so it should return immediately".
questions.promptHtml: Why is it slow, and what do you do? The product owner says "analytics must not delay the user, but we still want it to be sent".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The analytics SDK is slow, remove it." Or "Use GlobalScope.launch so it doesn't block." The second loses structure and cancellation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must analytics events survive the user leaving the screen? Is losing an event acceptable on process death? Is push.refreshRegistration safe to be cancelled? Which scope outlives the order screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by moving the two side effects out of the function. Short-term, a timeout on analytics isn't the answer, because it still delays confirmation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) coroutineScope waits for all children, including the launched ones, before it returns. The last line only produces the return value. The function returns when the slowest child ends: 400 + 6,000 ms = about 6.4 s, close to the observed 6.6 s. (b) The order API is slow: ruled out by its own p95 of 900 ms. (c) UI thread work: unlikely.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log a timestamp at the order assignment and at function return. A runTest with a fake slow analytics: the placeOrder result is delayed by virtual time of the slowest child.
  5. Root cause: Structured concurrency guarantees that nothing started inside a scope outlives it. "Fire and forget" is exactly what this structure forbids, and the code asks for it inside coroutineScope.
  6. Fix: The side effects belong to a longer-lived owner, an application scope, and the caller must not wait for them:
class OrderRepo(
    private val api: Api,
    private val appScope: CoroutineScope,   // SupervisorJob + Default; injected
    private val analytics: Analytics,
    private val push: Push,
) {
    suspend fun placeOrder(cart: Cart): Order {
        val order = api.placeOrder(cart)
        appScope.launch { runCatching { analytics.track(order) }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it } }
        appScope.launch { push.refreshRegistration() }
        return order
    }
}

Note the scope is injected and has a SupervisorJob, so an analytics failure doesn't kill the scope, and tests can substitute a test scope. Handle failures inside the children (or install a CoroutineExceptionHandler in the app scope) because launch failures in an app scope go to the uncaught handler. 7. Prevention: A review heuristic: "a launch inside coroutineScope is a parallel part of this function, not fire-and-forget". A test that proves the function returns before slow side effects finish (use virtual time with a never-completing fake). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not use GlobalScope, because it is untestable and hides ownership. I would not remove the structure by launch(Job()) in the function, which detaches the child and loses cancellation and errors. Trade-off: app-scope work isn't cancelled when the user leaves, which is what we want for analytics. For lossless delivery across process death, hand events to WorkManager or a local queue instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tests then become flaky? → Inject the scope, and in tests give it the TestScope's dispatcher. Assert side effects with advanceUntilIdle().
  • Could Dispatchers.Default app-scope work be starved by the slow SDK call (6 s)? → If the SDK blocks a thread, yes. Wrap blocking SDK calls with withContext(IO) and a timeout.
  • And on process death? → The event is lost unless it is persisted first. Write to a queue (Room) in the same transaction as the order, then flush.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout p95 regression of several seconds was traced to a third-party SDK inside a coroutineScope. The SDK's latency wasn't new; the code had always waited for it. Only the data-center move of the SDK vendor made it visible.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: expects the function to return at the last line, or suggests GlobalScope.
  • Hire: explains that scopes wait for children, and moves the work to an owned longer-lived scope.
  • Strong hire: also handles failure routing in the app scope, testability via injection, the blocking-SDK caveat, and durability on process death.

questions.contextHtml: A large app is migrating its data layer from callbacks and ExecutorService to coroutines. A legacy TokenProvider interface used by an OkHttp Authenticator (called on an OkHttp dispatcher thread) must stay synchronous: fun refreshToken(): String. The new implementation is suspend fun refresh(): String (uses Retrofit suspend plus DataStore). The migration PR implements the bridge as = runBlocking { refresh() }. During the staged rollout at 10%, the team observes: no ANR, no crash, but p99 API latency for the 10% group is 3x worse during token expiry waves, and some requests fail with java.net.SocketTimeoutException while the auth server shows few refresh calls. Thread dumps show many OkHttp Dispatcher threads parked in BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking.
questions.promptHtml: Is the bridge acceptable? How do you make it safe, and how do you roll it out?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "runBlocking is banned, rewrite OkHttp to coroutines now." A big-bang rewrite is not what a live migration allows. The other weak answer is "it's on a background thread, so fine".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many requests can hit a 401 at the same moment (the peak concurrency)? Does refresh() use Dispatchers.IO or Default? Does it take a lock or call OkHttp itself (same dispatcher)? What is the callTimeout? Is there already single-flight dedupe?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the flag back to 0%, or cap it, if the SocketTimeout rate is above the SLO. Keep the 10% data as the baseline for the second try.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Thundering herd: when a token expires, N parallel requests each get a 401, each calls the bridge, and each starts its own refresh. N parked OkHttp threads, N refresh calls (the server sees few because the refresh token rotates, so most fail or are rejected). (b) Starvation: OkHttp Dispatcher threads are parked, so new requests are queued behind them. OkHttp's maxRequests is 64 by default, and the parked authenticator threads consume that budget. (c) The refresh coroutine itself needs an OkHttp thread, because it uses the same client: a self-deadlock risk. Hence the SocketTimeoutException for the callers. (d) Dispatcher choice inside refresh(): if it uses Dispatchers.Default with a small pool, it is another starvation point.
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dumps (already available) count the parked threads. OkHttp's EventListener shows queue time. Server metrics show refresh attempts per second. A load test in staging with 200 parallel requests and an expired token.
  5. Root cause: A runBlocking bridge is tolerable as a syntax adapter, but this one has no bound, no dedupe, and shares a thread budget with the very work it waits for. During an expiry wave, 64 threads can be parked waiting for one refresh that itself needs a thread.
  6. Fix:
class BridgedTokenProvider(
    private val refresher: TokenRefresher,   // suspend; uses a separate OkHttpClient/dispatcher
    private val appScope: CoroutineScope,
) : TokenProvider {
    private val lock = Any()
    private var inFlight: Deferred<String>? = null

    override fun refreshToken(): String {
        val d = synchronized(lock) {
            inFlight ?: appScope.async { refresher.refresh() }
                .also { def -> inFlight = def; def.invokeOnCompletion { synchronized(lock) { inFlight = null } } }
        }
        return runBlocking { withTimeout(10_000) { d.await() } }   // bounded wait; the caller thread is an OkHttp thread
    }
}

Properties: only one refresh runs (single flight), the refresh uses its own client and scope so it does not need the blocked threads, the caller's wait is bounded, and a caller giving up (timeout) cancels only its await. The eventual full migration (an interceptor/authenticator written with a Mutex) is covered in the cross-cutting scenario on token refresh. 7. Prevention: a load test in CI for the expiry wave. A metric: parked-thread count and refresh calls per expiry. A lint rule that allows runBlocking only in classes annotated as bridges, with a required timeout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not do a big-bang rewrite of OkHttp usage mid-rollout. I would not remove the timeout "because refresh is fast": under an outage it is the safety valve. I would not run refresh() on the same OkHttp dispatcher. A bridge costs one parked thread per waiting request, so I'd ship it with a deprecation date.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why appScope.async rather than runBlocking { refresher.refresh() } directly? → So concurrent callers share one refresh, and one caller's timeout cannot cancel it for the others.
  • What if the refresh fails? → await() rethrows to every waiter. Map to IOException so OkHttp treats it as a network failure, and clear inFlight (done by invokeOnCompletion) so the next 401 retries.
  • Could interruption matter? → OkHttp may interrupt threads on cancel. runBlocking then cancels its coroutine (1.10.2 fixed an edge case where an interrupted runBlocking failed to run to completion, so use a current version).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bridge shipped to 5% looked healthy until the first long-lived-session day of the month, when many tokens expired together. The thread-dump signature, a wall of parked dispatcher threads, was recognised from an earlier incident, and single-flight plus a separate client fixed it in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: calls the bridge fine, or demands a full rewrite.
  • Hire: identifies the thundering herd and thread starvation, adds dedupe and a timeout.
  • Strong hire: finds the shared-thread-budget and self-deadlock risk, designs a bounded single-flight bridge with a separate client, specifies rollout metrics, and plans the removal of the bridge.
